Messages.Author: Greg Faulkner
Messages.Body:
In article <7hc2cp$4m7$1...@nnrp1.deja.com>, jt...@cornell.edu says...

>Rochester draft (as far as I know) usually refers to a Magic

>draft format. I think the way it works is that you put some
>cards in the middle of the table, face up, and people take
>turns picking a card from the ones available. In Magic, you
>do that for each booster until you're done. I wouldn't think
>it'd actually be a *bad* format for Jyhad, except that it might
>take a while to do the drafting.

If you are referring to the format where each person is given a finite amount
of "draft points" to spend on cards, then I have to say that I really enjoyed
that format. It is a little slow but it builds suspense (for example: will I
be able to get a Backways for the Gangrel deck I'm building?). More
importantly, it builds a more focused sealed deck. Sealed decks are always
supposed to have a lot of randomness to them, but it's nice to actually plan a
few cominations without having to depend on the luck of getting them in a
starter.

One drawback is that everyone else watches you as you draft (build) your deck.
It leaves little surprise in the actual gameplay, which is fine if you are in
a league (but bad for a tournament). On the other hand, watching other people
draft allows you to "play spoiler" and draft the cards other players need (I
like the spoiler part).

The major problem I have with this format is that the seating is fixed and the
person drafting directly in front of you could be trying to build the same deck
as you. In that particular case, you are forced to choose an alternate
strategy. Perhaps seating arrangements should be switched between boosters.

Greg

Messages.Author: L. Scott Johnson
Messages.Body:
jt...@cornell.edu (Joshua Duffin) writes:
>Rochester draft (as far as I know) usually refers to a Magic
>draft format. I think the way it works is that you put some
>cards in the middle of the table, face up, and people take
>turns picking a card from the ones available. In Magic, you
>do that for each booster until you're done. I wouldn't think
>it'd actually be a *bad* format for Jyhad, except that it might
>take a while to do the drafting.

Shawn Carnes ran a tournament of this format at Gen*Con '96.
One starter and two boosters - you open and evaluate your starter
and then draft the boosters. Each player takes one card from the
top of their booster supply (still in the order it was in the pack)
and puts it face-up on the table. Each player in turn then picks
one of those cards. Repeat, reversing the order. Then repeat again,
with the next player starting the draft. And so on.

Build your deck (40 - 90 cards) from your starter and the cards
you drafted. (60 card minimums are really only necessary for
unlimited formats.)

It worked pretty well, as far as I can remember.

I'm not familiar with the 'points' angle. The version I've
heard of just has people take turns choosing a card from the
array of cards in the center of the table. I agree that it's
good to reduce the randomness of sealed somewhat; Michigan draft
tries to do the same but with fewer cards in the draft (last
I heard).

> One drawback is that everyone else watches you as you draft (build)
your deck.
> It leaves little surprise in the actual gameplay, which is fine if
you are in
> a league (but bad for a tournament). On the other hand, watching
other people
> draft allows you to "play spoiler" and draft the cards other players
need (I
> like the spoiler part).

I would think there could still be surprise in a tournament
if you play against people you didn't draft with. And then,
even though you draft things you want to use, I would expect
that the decks built will probably be unfocused enough as
to produce some surprises in gameplay.

The "hate draft" aspect is cool too, yeah, although in
sealed it's probably pretty often just as much to get the good
card for yourself as it is to keep some particular opponent from
having it.

> The major problem I have with this format is that the seating is
fixed and the
> person drafting directly in front of you could be trying to build the
same deck
> as you. In that particular case, you are forced to choose an
alternate
> strategy. Perhaps seating arrangements should be switched between
boosters.

I think drafts like this often reverse the order of card selection
each booster/each round? Although you're still sitting between
the same people, yes.

Sounds like Noal tried a version of this that he didn't like,
and you and L Scott tried versions that you did like. Guess
I'll just have to find out for myself.

Josh
